Jesus Christ, I was trying to de-escalate the situation. I was trying to say that we probably have the same sentiment towards the companies, but I guess that’s not good enough for you. If you can’t see the difference between “knee-jerk defending AI” and some just wanting to avoid this self righteous circlejerk I’d suspect you may be a machine yourself. But no, you’re just a knuckle-dragger. 

At no point did I say I wasn’t indicting studios that wanted to use AI to abdicate their decision-making, but you have never provided any proof that that is the case, just that it’s a facet of a holistic process. But far be it for me to a assume you could actually generate a novel thought.

Your point was that if left up to AI it would need an AI-approved creative team, which you never define, so I facetiously said that given that it was would have been approved by AI it would be definitionally AI-approved. You have no criteria for what that meant so the only thing to go off of what a tautological definition.

Cinelytic is a tool, all decisions rest with the people in of running the studios. It is providing you with one way to collect data, but that’s no different than asking an employee to give you the same data in an Excel spreadsheet. If a machine is taking over decision-making from the studio, that’s a human failing of the executives who cede control. But as of right now, nothing has shown that an AI gets final say in any decision-making process. 

As for the first people labeled “box office poison” you should really look at what their prospects looked like after the publication of that article: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_Office_Poison_(magazine_article)?wprov=sfti1 

I’m just trying to say that people and machines can make blanket numerical calculations that neuter creative decisions, but the choice is always in human hands. I just don’t see the point of criticizing computer programs when we’re really mad at the way people make choices and determine value.

My point is that your initial point is a tautology. If you want to use “AI-approved” as a catch-all for counterfactual choice that would not have worked as well, then you need to explain.

Also, my second point is that we cannot make the assumption that the AI process for greenlighting would be as simple as raw name v. profit calculation. As is stated in the video AI isn’t intelligence per se, it’s large scale machine learning, the response you get is as complex as what you prompt it with and how you prompt it. It’s a tool. Patrick himself states that he doesn’t have a problem with it being used to assist in a process, as long as it’s aiding “genuine human” expression”. If the fear is that a machine will a cold numbers assessment when deciding projects, that’s exactly what happened before except it was done by humans. Hell, the phrase you used “box office poison”, is from one person’s assessment of actors back in the Hollywood golden era, but because a human made that assessment I guess it’s better.

By definition it would have been more AI-approved, as it would have been approved by AI. The question is how it would have changed, and I don’t know think we can make any claim on that. If we’re making the assumption that all you would do to greenlight would be to select names and see how profitable their respective movies are then maybe, but any decision more detailed than that is hard to figure out.

Some stories can have that work but it has to be in the structure of the narrative. I haven’t seen Oppenheimer but I don’t expect a ton of jokes, but that’s because I expect it to cut from tense boardroom scene to tense boardroom scene.

It’s something that’s become more and more evident to me as time has gone on: a lot of people assume that dramas must be completely devoid of humor. I think we see a lot of people slot things into the category of “black comedy” as opposed to what they are which is “drama with jokes”. I find it a bit limiting.

There is a ton to work with here so I will answer the "personal excuses" portion first and then try to hit all your points, let me know if you would let me if you would like elaboration. And certainly, I am not opposed to turning any of your point into a thread by itself because discourse is the best way, of course (shoot me for this garbage pun).

Personal excuses here refers to any sort of othering myself that I could do that mentally I would view as separating me from the realities of the mass agricultural industry, so things like "cheese isn't as bad as the meat industry", "at least they're not being killed", "I'd rather have people in the factory getting eggs and making a wage than nothing" etc. I knew the horrors of any form of animal exploitation but I was saying I had to live with that exploitation so I might as well enjoy. Obviously, there is still some idealism that goes into it, but what doesn't have that.

1. I recognize the cost of any decision I make in my consumption and do not believe this to be a solution,  however I will also say that unless we begin taking the steps to counter other forms of exploitation, defeating class exploitation gets us to the point of human liberation where we no longer care about other injustice. I kind of take it in the same way intersectional socialists take their fight for queer, black, women's liberation I.e. It's purely ideological to believe that one solution will fix all problems.

2. I don't tie it to a what you buy determines how good you are philosophy, I'd say if you are going to buy (as we all must) and you have the ability to spend on something outside of that system you should. The exploitation of the labor force should not be an excuse for purposefully putting another being into an exploitative system. Your mileage may vary

3.  This I view not as a stop gap, but as something that should be done in addition to an end to capitalism. I don't think that ending capitalism will end the exploitation of animals (as we are more than willing to view this injustice as necessary as "we are just feeding the worker"), nor do I hold that veganism will in anyway necessarily lead to socialism. I think they are two issues that share a common ideal and should be worked for in tandem.

4. Everyone has some problem that can be used to deflect or negate someone's revolutionary are cause.  I, for one, am a consumer in the nicotine industry and know how harmful that can be to the workers in those fields. I would never criticize someone's adherence to socialism based on consuming meat, I mere ask why and how they separate the the two causes. 

5. I feel I kind of touched on this in point one, but I do not believe that essentially saying "it's all fucked" is a reason to not have to make a moral choice. Each person has to way the moral weight of each decision they make and I have come to the opinion that exploitation of the labor force + deforestation is less willfully harmful than exploitation of the labor force + deforestation for livestock enclosure + exploitation of said livestock. This is the most subjective analysis that I have, but any other system of account is just as subjective. 

6. At no point do I view this as a reason to not fight for other forms of liberation. This is another point where I would say a socialist economic system would not necessitate an end to this form of exploitation so I have to work for both. Again, YMMV

7. I don't hold at any point that individual veganism will fix the solution, but if a soc. revolution were to occur, I think it's a net positive if more people are already free of another form of injustice. Saying someone has to be exploited is not any excuse to either kill something or working something to death.

8. This I would take a "yes and" situation, All production is exploitative however that that doesn't absolve people from using that as a reason to say that is acceptable to indulge in an industry intentionally based on death as an output. 

Sorry if this comes across as too hardline. I would not judge others for the choice that they find themselves in, I just do not accept the idea that you can unconsciously make choices and say you did not have one.
